children: By Kelly Cloonan and Connor Hart
CrowdStrike Holdings and Zscaler both reported higher quarterly revenue on surging demand for cloud protection and tools designed to secure artificial-intelligence agents.

The results--which also prompted CrowdStrike to raise its full-year outlook--came as the two cybersecurity companies announced an agreement for CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in an all-stock swap valued at around $43.9 billion.
Combining the two businesses will give the merged entity more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue at closing, the companies said.

For the third quarter, CrowdStrike swung to a profit of $24.9 million, or 2 cents a share, from a loss of $26.8 million, or 3 cents a share, a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share were 34 cents, beating analyst estimates of 31 cents, according to FactSet.

Revenue climbed 28% to $1.58 billion, surpassing analysts' expectations of $1.53 billion. Annual recurring revenue grew 27% year over year to $6.26 billion, including $419.2 million in net new ARR added during the quarter.

CrowdStrike Chief Executive George Kurtz called the period the best quarter in the company's history, highlighting accelerated growth across the business and particular traction for its cybersecurity offering for AI agents.

For the full year, CrowdStrike now guides for revenue of about $6.08 billion, up from its prior forecast of about $5.99 billion to $6.01 billion. It projects adjusted earnings per share of $1.28, up from $1.25 to $1.26 previously.
Zscaler, meanwhile, posted a fiscal first-quarter loss of $27.4 million, or 17 cents a share, widening from a loss of $11.6 million, or 7 cents a share, a year earlier.
Stripping out one-time items, Zscaler earned $1.23 a share, ahead of the $1.16 a share expected by analysts polled by FactSet.
Revenue rose 20% to $949.3 million, ahead of Wall Street models for $937.7 million, while its annual recurring revenue increased 21% to $3.88 billion.

"AI is driving the most significant security transformation in our lifetime - it is rapidly uncovering hidden vulnerabilities and enabling malicious actors to execute automated exploits at unprecedented speed and scale, causing organizations to rethink how to defend against autonomous AI agents," Zscaler Chief Executive Jay Chaudhry said.
